source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Screen when the client reports persistent sadness, loss of interest, or another symptom suggesting a postpartum mood disorder.","B":"Omit postpartum screening if depression screening was already completed during pregnancy.","C":"Refer all mood screening to a mental-health specialist rather than using validated tools in obstetric care.","D":"Screen for depression and anxiety with a validated instrument and have systems for timely assessment and follow-up."}}
source_row.rationale: ACOG recommends screening patients receiving postpartum care for depression and anxiety with standardized, validated instruments and having systems in place for timely assessment, treatment, and follow-up. Option D matches that guidance even when the client does not volunteer symptoms. Option A incorrectly limits screening to symptomatic clients. Option B omits recommended postpartum screening. Option C incorrectly removes screening from routine obstetric care.
source_row.source_detail: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 4 / Patient Screening — screen everyone receiving postpartum care for depression and anxiety using standardized validated instruments, with systems for assessment, treatment, monitoring and follow-up. ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 4, June 2023, retained as current guidance; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Health Promotion and Maintenance; preventive care, screening, prenatal/postpartum and newborn health-promotion activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: ACOG — Patient Screening for Perinatal Mental Health
source_row.stem: At a routine postpartum visit, the client says mood is “fine” and reports no psychiatric history. Which approach to depression and anxiety screening is appropriate?
